speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (a) whether Singapore has received any updates on the Johor government's efforts to manage their hotspots and, if so, what are these; (b) how can the health and well-being of Singapore's residents be safeguarded against the long-term exposure to haze pollutants; and (c) whether there are plans to conduct outreach programmes to allay concerns and provide regular updates on the haze situation arising from hotspots in Johor.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Members of this House would be aware of the environmental pollution incidents in Johor over the last two months.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In February, the National Environment Agency (NEA) detected hotspots of fires with smoke plumes in Southern Johor through satellite remote sensing.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Department of Environment (DOE) Johor, subsequently alerted NEA to fires at two landfills in Bandar Tenggara and Tanjong Langsat, as well as a fire at Punggai in the area of an oil palm plantation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The resultant smoke plumes, blown by the prevailing northeasterly winds, affected both Johoreans and Singaporeans with intermittent burning smells over the past few weeks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: While most of the fires have been put out, NEA continued to detect hotspots in southern Johor.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA monitors the ambient air quality in Singapore through a network of real-time ambient air monitoring sensors across Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These sensors continuously measure the key air pollutants, namely, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, ozone, particulate matter of both PM2.5 and PM10.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The concentrations of these air pollutants are used to compute the Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) over a rolling 24-hour period.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Since June 2016, NEA has introduced bands and descriptors for the one-hour PM2.5 concentrations, as a guide to help the public better assess the current air quality.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The 24-hour PSI and the one-hour PM2.5 readings in the five regions of Singapore and corresponding health advisory are available to the public on the NEA website and myEnv mobile application.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Members of the public can use the information as a guide to plan their activities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Between early-February and mid-March when the hotspots were detected in Johor, the 24-hour PSI readings remained within the Good to Moderate range, and the one-hour PM2.5 levels remained in the Normal range.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hazardous fumes caused severe symptoms, including nausea, shortness of breath and vomiting.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Thousands needed immediate medical attention and many were admitted to hospitals for treatment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Some were in critical condition and had to be placed under intensive care.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Young and vulnerable children were among the worst affected.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The authorities closed all 111 schools in the Pasir Gudang district on 13 March 2019 for more than two weeks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Singaporeans watched with deep concern and were saddened by this serious environmental violation, where toxic chemicals were dumped into the river, with little regard for the people who live in the surrounding areas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The chemicals detected in the air samples from Sungai Kim Kim and its vicinity contained chemicals, such as benzene, which is carcinogenic.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Malaysian media has also reported illegal dumping of chemical waste at other sites in Pasir Gudang.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: According to the Malaysian authorities, they have cleaned up a 1.5 kilometres (km) polluted stretch of Sungai Kim Kim in Pasir Gudang.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Malaysian authorities have worked expeditiously to contain the problem, in view of the impact to the environment and to public health.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I wish all those affected, in particular, the children, a speedy recovery.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Singapore stands ready to provide assistance to the Malaysian authorities if needed.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Throughout this period, our agencies have been closely monitoring the situation and putting in place precautionary measures to guard against any potential pollution impacts arising from the illegal dumping of chemical waste.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have not detected any pollution impacts on Singapore’s air and water quality or water supply.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA continuously monitors the ambient concentration of a variety of Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) at our air monitoring stations, including at four stations located in the north-eastern region of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These include benzene, toluene and xylene, as well as other common VOCs from industrial emissions which are also closely monitored by other environmental agencies, such as the United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA).

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA has not detected any elevated levels of VOCs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The 24-hour PSI has also been in the Good to Low-Moderate range, while the one-hour PM2.5 readings remained in the Normal range.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) has also deployed its portable stand-off chemical gas detectors at the northeast region of Singapore to detect toxic chemicals and has not detected any toxic chemicals in the air.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For water quality, NEA’s continuous buoy-based coastal water quality monitoring sensors deployed along the Straits of Johor have not detected any unusual variation in the key physical, chemical and microbiological water quality parameters.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA has also taken the additional step of collecting water samples at Pulau Ubin and its vicinity to test additional parameters, including compounds Malaysia has identified due to the chemical waste dumped in Sungai Kim Kim.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These compounds have not been detected in our water samples.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA has also not detected any anomalies in the quality of the waters at our recreational coastal beaches.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Public Utilities Board's (PUB’s) online sensors have shown that the water quality of Johor River, our waterways and reservoirs in the north and north-eastern part of Singapore, as well as the water supply is within normal variations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Onsite inspections and water quality checks have also shown no abnormalities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This incident has no impact on our water supply as the chemical dumping location is outside of our Johor River catchment area, where part of our water supply comes from.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There have been no reports of unusual fish mortality at our local fish farms in the Straits of Johor.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Environment pollution is a cross-border issue that requires collaboration between the authorities of both countries.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These include the provision of early warnings and environmental monitoring data and guidelines.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA and SCDF have been in contact with their respective Malaysian counterparts – DOE Johor and the Johor Fire and Rescue Department (BOMBA) – to obtain regular updates on the situation there.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to monitor the situation and provide updates if there are any significant developments.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will also continue to step up our checks and enforcement to protect our environment and safeguard the health and safety of Singaporeans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Over the last one month, residents in Yishun Town had to suffer not just the burning smell, but on two days at least, there were also pungent smells like sewer pipes bursting.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many residents have been asking me what happened.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The second question is that my residents have also given constant feedback that they saw chimneys burning in Pasir Gudang and they are worried about the long-term effects on their health.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Every night, they see these chimneys burning and they are thinking, "Surely, there are gases being given out." I would like to ask the Ministry whether there is any long-term effect on the health of residents.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For the first question on whether we can give more regular updates, first of all, as I have said, on the NEA website as well as on the myENV app, we do provide readings, hourly updates, in fact, of PSI and PM2.5.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We monitor that for the five regions – north, south, east, west and central.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: If there are any significant variations, for instance, above normal levels, unhealthy levels, we would notify the public with this information.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to cross-border environmental pollution, for instance, or smell coming from Johor, we work very closely with our Johor counterparts, that is, DOE Johor and also the Johor BOMBA.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We also have continuous monitoring as well as our remote satellite sensing to identify smoke plumes as well as hotspots.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But these, obviously, would be for the larger hotspots and smoke plumes that we can detect and, depending on the wind direction, whether they will actually travel down to Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, for the recent early February to mid-March incidents, because of the northeasterly winds, fires normally occurred in the afternoon.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: By the time it comes in in the evening when the wind has weakened or slowed down, as well as the temperatures have cooled, these smells, if there are, would be harder to dilute and disperse because it will be hard to disperse the air pollutants upwards due to the cooler temperature and then the wind does not take it away.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, there may be smells but ambient air quality may be alright.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And in this case, we have found throughout the period that ambient air quality based on PSI and PM2.5 has been in the normal to moderate range and PM2.5 reading is normal.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The smells can be due to a variety of reasons, depending on whether it is a plantation burning or landfill burning.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: By themselves, there could be smell or they could be mixed with other chemicals and different smells are produced.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But as I have said, there is generally no correlation between the air quality readings and the smells.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Regarding flaring – I assume that is what the Member is talking about – there are petrochemical industries in Pasir Gudang.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And flaring is a common safety feature in refineries and petrochemical plants.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: What happens is, during routine maintenance, or when there is either a plant shutdown or startup, you need flaring to prevent the build-up of process gases.
